questions.question: What do the inventory.gc_pressure (log:inventory.gc_pressure) and cart.inventory_refused (log:cart.inventory_refused) entries reveal about service health between minutes 30‑35?
Show error_rate and latency_p99 trends for web (metric:web:error_rate:31), cart (metric:cart:error_rate:31), and inventory (metric:inventory:latency_p99:30) from minute 28 to 36.
Were any deploys to inventory, web, or cache recorded around minute 30‑36 besides the known cart deploy d5 (deploy:d5)?

findings.text: inventory.gc_pressure logs appear from minute 32 (15 occurrences) showing heap at 75% and 620 ms GC pauses, matching the sharp rise in inventory latency (p99 ≈ 409 ms) and error rate, indicating memory pressure degrading health.

cart.inventory_refused logs start at minute 34 (2,231 occurrences) reporting "inventory unavailable: connection refused", mirroring cart’s error‑rate jump and showing downstream impact of the failing inventory service.
Inventory latency_p99 spiked at minute 30 (fault minute), rising from ~213ms baseline to 409ms, the earliest divergence in the chain.
Web error_rate stayed near baseline until minute 34, spiking to 0.3904 then dropping by minute 35.
Cart error_rate followed, spiking to 0.5568 at minute 34 after a gradual rise from minute 31, recovering by minute 35.
The inventory-prefetch flag was turned on by ops at minute 30, coinciding with the latency rise and later GC pressure.
Inventory suffered OOMKilled at minute 34, causing connection refusals in cart and error spikes in web and cart.
No deploys to inventory, web, or cache were recorded between minutes 30 and 36; the only deploy in the summary is cart deploy d5 at minute 16.

hypotheses.summary: Inventory service shows rising memory usage, GC pressure, and OOM after enabling the inventory-prefetch flag, indicating a memory leak triggered by the prefetch feature.
Turning on inventory-prefetch may have increased request load, but saturation did not rise, making overload less likely.
Cart error spikes follow inventory failures, suggesting inventory as a slow provider.
Web error rises after cart and inventory issues, indicating downstream propagation.
No clear root cause identified from available data.

data.rationale: Disabling the inventory-prefetch flag removes the trigger for the extra memory allocation that caused the leak, addressing the root cause rather than merely alleviating symptoms.

prose.summary: A memory leak in the inventory component was injected at minute 30, triggering an alert at minute 34. Investigation identified the leak, and the inventory-prefetch feature was disabled at minute 66, restoring service health by minute 70.
prose.rootCause: Memory leak in the inventory service, exacerbated by the inventory-prefetch feature.
prose.whatWentWell: Alert fired promptly, investigation started quickly, hypothesis ranking identified the issue, and the remediation (disabling prefetch) was approved and applied within minutes, leading to SLO recovery.
actionItems: Add continuous memory usage monitoring for the inventory service.
Audit and fix the inventory-prefetch code to prevent leaks.
Create an automated remediation to restart or disable inventory-prefetch on leak detection.
Update runbooks to include memory‑leak detection and remediation steps.
